doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Defining the groove
summary: Roker defines groove as the feeling of the blues that audiences visibly share, at any tempo, with a pulse.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Let me ask you an elusive word, and you just give me your definition of it however you can. Try to define for me the word groove.

Groove. Groove to me is a blues, a term that depicts the blues. And when you’re playing and you look at an audience and everybody is groovin’. And you look in the audience man and you see everybody doing this, that’s groove, that’s a groove. But if you’re playing something and everybody’s talking, that’s no groove. A groove man, when a player plays, when a band plays or a player, it can be a solo guy by himself, two guys, ten guys, but it’s the feeling. See that’s the feeling of the blues. It’s the groove. And you’re playing man, and it doesn’t matter what tempo it is, but usually a groove tempo is, when they say a groove, the tempo is usually a moderate tempo. But that’s not, you can groove in any tempo. But basically people think of a groove when you say a groove tempo, and you look at an audience man, and people are — that’s what groove means.
In other words there’s a communication going on there.

Oh yeah. You can communicate without being a groove. Now because sometimes you can play, you can play rubato -- without tempo, you know what I mean? And you can communicate. But when you groove, there’s a pulse, there’s a pulse happening man. And people feel it man. And you know they feel it man because you can see ‘em.
